findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. On their own, the opening lines answer "what is this" and "why it matters".
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next step is linked from the top of the page, and the Next steps section gives concrete commands (clone, ./setup.sh, athena ask "add a changelog"). A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The prerequisites come after the clone step. They belong first. The page also never says whether a paid Claude account or API key is needed, or roughly what a run costs.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone ..." listed before "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: The lede promises a second-model check and per-step costs, but this page shows neither. No verdict or cost is given for the study itself, so a newcomer sees the promise without seeing it kept here.
findings.source: Lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost"

findings.text: Someone who came to learn about Athena lands on a page that is almost all a detailed state machine of another project. The lede explains why, but the link between "request in, commit out" and "a study" is left for the reader to work out.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the States, Transitions and Claims sections

findings.text: The Start here section and the "Words used first" list give a good on-ramp into firstmate. The plain one-line definition of firstmate and the step-by-step walk through one piece of work are easy to follow.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails"

findings.text: Some terms in the cards and claims never appear in the glossary: captain-held inventory, endpoint, crewmate, heartbeat and charter. A newcomer reading the transitions will hit words they cannot look up.
findings.source: Transition t11 guard: "its captain-held inventory is verified"; t8: "a secondmate with no endpoint"; c41: "leaves its own crewmates running"

findings.text: The glossary entry for "ship" is weak because it defines the word by where it appears. The "What firstmate is" section gives a better definition: "A ship changes a project".
findings.source: Glossary: "ship — A kind of task, named next to scouts."

findings.text: The state list gives only names and tags, with no description on each line. A reader has to go back to the intro paragraph or the glossary to learn what each state means.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "ready waiting" … "close-pending waiting"

findings.text: These lines are for the repository owner, not a visitor. A newcomer will not know which owner is meant or where the studies/ folder lives.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision"; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/"

findings.text: Stating the study's limits openly helps trust, and the claims linked to pinned source lines show the traceability the lede promises. Still, f3 reads like internal process notes to a first-time visitor.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..." and f1: "every claim is marked read"
